# Prediction, Generation, and Optimization for Architecture Design {#sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"But they are useless. They can only give you answers."*
>
> Pablo Picasso, *The Paris Review* (1964) [@Fifield1964Picasso]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Picasso was speaking about the calculating machines of his
day, but his complaint still identifies the approach-selection problem. A tool
can return an answer without asking whether the study needed that answer,
whether a simpler calculation would have settled the question, or whether the
project can afford to check it. Architects have to ask those questions before
choosing an approach.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
Which engineering job needs help, is AI assistance warranted, and what is the
smallest sufficient approach that retains a named check and fallback?
:::

An approach choice begins with the architecture problem, not with a model. If a
cache study has three legal capacities and each can be evaluated affordably,
direct tool runs may settle the comparison. If thousands of existing
configurations compete for a few expensive simulations, a predictor may screen
them or an optimizer may choose which ones to run. If the required RTL, test,
kernel, or compiler schedule does not yet exist, generation may construct a
candidate. These are different jobs.

The same distinction applies inside larger systems. A foundation model may
supply reusable prior knowledge, retrieval may supply current project context,
and an agent may request tools and react to their returns. Those components do
not form new peer method families, and none makes generation the default. The
architect still has to decide which operation the job requires, whether a
conventional, learned, or hybrid technique should perform it, whether several
components must be composed, or whether direct tool use is enough.

Fit depends on more than the desired output. The available data, legal search
space, evaluator, feedback cost, runtime latency, confidentiality constraints,
required reliability, reversibility, and consequence of failure can all change
the answer. A method that saves simulator calls may still lose once model
setup, licensed tools, checking, and expert review are counted. A powerful
generator may be the wrong choice when a compiler pass or parameterized
template already constructs the artifact safely.

The durable rule is to choose the smallest sufficient approach. Name the
engineering role first, choose a family and concrete technique only when they
fit, and keep a real evaluator or check able to reject the output. The chapter
develops that choice through prediction, generation, optimization, and their
combinations, then applies it to constrained kernel construction, compiler
tuning, and the Lighthouse cache study.

This chapter selects and composes methods. It uses an illustrative pre-review
tool-path capacity model to diagnose whether the declared tools can absorb
candidate work. It does not specify runtime queue implementation, retries, or
wrappers, which belong to
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces. It also does not decide what a
measurement proves, which belongs to @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Distinguish an engineering role, method family, concrete technique, and
  composed system.
- Select the smallest sufficient approach from the architecture question,
  available evidence, evaluator or check, cost, and failure consequences.
- Select among predictive, generative, and optimization techniques by the work
  each must perform, the structure it assumes, and where its applicable
  conditions end.
- Compose conventional, predictive, generative, and optimization components
  without assuming a fixed order, and preserve external checks and a viable
  fallback.
- Justify a method decision using total cost, feedback limits, and the
  consequence of failure.

:::

## Roles and Methods Answer Different Questions

Architecture work can require constructing a missing artifact, estimating an
expensive consequence, selecting an experiment, or checking a claimed
property. The first decision is whether that work needs a new component. If
the candidates are known and their evaluations are affordable, adding a
predictor, generator, or optimizer creates setup and review work without
removing the limiting work.

The *smallest sufficient approach* is the least elaborate approach that
performs the required engineering job while preserving the evaluator and later
checks. It minimizes total work, not code length or inference cost. Choosing no
added method is therefore a positive engineering decision when direct
evaluation costs less and preserves the required checks.

Consider the three cache capacities used in the Lighthouse study. The
engineering job is to compare already known candidates. Direct simulation and
an SRAM model fit the available budget, so no new prediction, generation, or
optimization method is needed. If the study instead had thousands of legal
capacities and organizations, its job might become screening, its family might
be prediction, its technique might be a calibrated regression model, and its
composition would still end in the simulator and physical checks. The job,
family, technique, and composition answer different questions.

The four levels in @tbl-role-by-stall-mode form a non-exhaustive working
vocabulary rather than a literature consensus or a prescription for an
agent's internal organization. Roles remain externally inspectable through
their inputs, outputs, and next checks. The other levels identify the broad
operation, concrete mechanism, and complete study composition.

| **Decision layer** | **Question** | **Choices** | **Required discipline** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Engineering role** | What work must be done? | Propose, screen, search, critique, repair, check, explain, or coordinate. | Name the input, expected output, limits, and next check for each role. |
| **Method family** | What broad operation performs the role? | Prediction, generation, optimization, or another operation the problem requires. These families are useful but not exhaustive and may be combined. | Select the operation from the required output and feedback rather than forcing a fixed sequence. |
| **Technique** | What concrete mechanism fits the artifact and feedback? | A conventional, learned, or hybrid technique, such as an analytical model, regression, Gaussian process, graph neural network, large language model, Bayesian optimizer, solver, compiler pass, or heuristic. | State the assumptions, applicable conditions, cost, and failure conditions of the actual technique. |
| **System composition** | Which components must work together? | One technique and a tool, or several generators, predictors, optimizers, conventional and learned techniques, retrieval components, and tools. | Give every component a distinct input, output, cost, and check. |

: **Choose the smallest approach that performs the needed work.** The four
levels keep the role, method family, concrete technique, and system composition
separate. {#tbl-role-by-stall-mode tbl-colwidths="[20,30,25,25]"}

Keeping these decisions separate prevents a model label from standing in for
the work it performs, its support, or the cost it adds.

An engineering role is clear only when it returns something that the next part
of the study can inspect. This lecture names eight such roles. Proposal and
repair create candidate state. Screening and search allocate scarce
evaluation. Critique, checking, and explanation diagnose or establish
properties. Coordination connects those jobs without replacing them.
@tbl-method-role-handoffs fixes the meaning of each role through its output and
next handoff rather than through the software or person performing it.

| **Engineering role** | **Concrete output** | **Next check or handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proposal** | A named candidate, artifact, or experiment request with the changed fields identified. | Check legality and scope before invoking an expensive tool. |
| **Screening** | A scoped estimate or ranking with its predicted property, applicable conditions, and uncertainty. | Send selected candidates to the declared measurement path and retain predictions for calibration. |
| **Search** | The next candidate or experiment, its selection basis, and the remaining budget. | Hand the request to the environment without changing the objective or legal design space. |
| **Critique** | A testable defect, missing assumption, or conflict tied to a named artifact or claim. | Return it to the role that owns the revision; critique neither changes the candidate nor replaces the requested check. |
| **Repair** | A revised artifact or request linked to its parent and the change made. | Treat it as a new candidate and rerun checks whose inputs or assumptions changed. |
| **Checking** | A result from a named check for a named property and condition, including incomplete or unknown outcomes. | Hand the result to @sec-feedback-verification-trust to determine what it measured and what conclusion it can support. |
| **Explanation** | A proposed mechanism and the observations or alternatives it must distinguish. | Request a targeted contrast or measurement; do not substitute the explanation for a property check. |
| **Coordination** | An ordered set of requests with dependencies, budgets, artifacts, and candidate identifiers. | Hand the requests to the environment, which constructs and executes the tool requests. |

: **Roles become useful when their outputs and next handoffs are explicit.**
The role names describe engineering work. Prediction, generation, and
optimization describe broad operations, while conventional, learned, and
hybrid techniques provide concrete ways to perform them.
{#tbl-method-role-handoffs tbl-colwidths="[18,40,42]"}

Method families do not identify a software package or map one-to-one to roles.
Prediction estimates a property or later state, generation constructs an
artifact or candidate, and optimization chooses among actions or candidates.
Concrete techniques include enumerators, analytical models, solvers, compiler
passes, and heuristics, as well as regression, Gaussian processes, graph neural
networks, and large language models (LLMs). Conventional, learned, and hybrid
describe how such a technique performs the work. They are not concrete
techniques or peer method families. A compiler can construct and check
transformations, while Bayesian optimization combines a predictor with an
evaluation-selection procedure.

*No added method* names the study-level choice to proceed directly. It does not
describe the internals of declared tools, which may already contain estimation
or search. The complete workflow may omit AI entirely when conventional tools
perform every needed role more economically and reliably. `XR-L2-CAP-A`, the
represented three-capacity cache study, already includes `SRAM-A`, the declared
SRAM area, timing, and energy model, in its tool path. Its fixed threshold is an
SRAM screen rather than a newly selected component that proposes, predicts, or
searches the study requests.

A learned correction to an analytical latency model is a hybrid technique.
Placing that predictor inside an optimizer creates a
prediction-plus-optimization composition that still needs an external
evaluator.

Foundation models, agents, and retrieval occupy this component level. An
architecture foundation model can supply representations or prior knowledge
used by a predictor, generator, optimizer, or coordinating component.
Retrieval can supply current specifications, code, or examples to another
technique. An agent can request actions, read returns, and select another
action. They are components or supporting capabilities, not peer families
beside prediction, generation, and optimization.

@fig-role-method-map summarizes the distinctions without assigning one method
family to one role.

![**An engineering role does not determine one method family.** Begin with the work the study needs and decide whether direct tool use is sufficient. If an added method is justified, select prediction, generation, optimization, or another family, then choose a concrete conventional, learned, or hybrid mechanism. Every path must end in an inspectable output and a named next check.](images/F5d-role-method-map){#fig-role-method-map width="100%" fig-alt="Four-stage map. Eight engineering roles connect through a many-to-many relationship to prediction, generation, optimization, and another method family, with a direct-tool option. The technique panel groups representative concrete mechanisms as conventional, learned, or hybrid. Every path ends with an inspectable output and a named next check."}

Engineering roles and method families have a many-to-many relationship, and a
role can proceed directly to a tool when no added method is justified
(@fig-role-method-map). A role names the work rather than a model. Proposal
therefore does not always require generation, screening does not always require
prediction, and search does not require a learned optimizer. When the work does
justify an added method, representative mechanisms may be conventional, such as
enumerators, solvers, compiler passes, and heuristics; learned, such as
regression, Gaussian processes, graph neural networks, and LLMs; or hybrid,
such as an analytical model with a learned correction. Every choice must
produce an inspectable output and name a check that can reject or redirect it.
These choices do not impose a fixed order among method families.

The practical differences appear in familiar architecture work. If an RTL
fragment, test bench, or candidate configuration is missing, generation can
propose one, but the project must pay to check it. If simulation is too
expensive to run on every existing candidate, prediction can estimate or rank a
decision-relevant consequence, but the project must pay for calibration and
later confirmation. If too many legal configurations compete for a limited
evaluation budget, optimization can select the next candidate or experiment,
but the project must define the objective and pay for the search. These
conditions suggest a family but do not select a technique. The limiting work
and its conditions determine the fit.

## Method Choice Begins With the Limiting Work

One sequence governs the method choice. It begins with the architecture
decision and direct or conventional options, identifies the limiting work, and
rejects any approach whose support, evaluator, cost, fallback, or stopping
condition is inadequate. The artifact, legal space, feedback, and deployment
tests below supply the information that sequence requires.

### A Conditional Selection Guide

Use the following sequence before selecting any added method.

1. State the architecture decision, comparator, objectives, constraints, and
   concrete output that the work must produce.
2. Ask whether direct evaluation, a conventional algorithm, solver, compiler
   analysis, heuristic, or parameterized generator can settle the question
   within the available budget.
3. Identify the limiting work. Candidate construction points toward generation;
   expensive outcome measurement points toward prediction; selecting among
   too many legal alternatives points toward optimization.
4. If actions change later state, decide whether a transition-aware predictor
   or sequential optimizer is needed. Do not introduce either when candidates
   can be evaluated independently.
5. If measurement, checking, or review is already the bottleneck, improve that
   path or reduce the work arriving at it. Producing more candidates cannot
   repair a saturated evaluator.
6. Reject the proposed method when its data, representation, legal actions,
   evaluator, support, total cost, fallback, or stopping condition is
   inadequate.

@fig-method-selection-guide turns that sequence into a conditional choice
rather than a fixed order among prediction, generation, and optimization.

![**Method choice begins with the limiting work.** Direct evaluation or a conventional method remains the first option when it can settle the decision within the required cost and time. Otherwise, one or more shortages may point toward generation, prediction, optimization, a transition-aware method, or a composition. A saturated checking path calls for fewer arrivals or better checking, not more candidates. Every route ends at a named check matched to the consequence, a fallback, and a stopping rule.](images/F5e-method-selection-guide){#fig-method-selection-guide width="100%" fig-alt="Conditional method-selection flow. The architecture decision and output lead to a test of whether direct evaluation or a conventional method is sufficient. If not, one or more limiting forms of work point toward generation, prediction, optimization, transition-aware methods, or improving a saturated checking path. Every branch ends at declared support, total cost, a named check matched to the consequence, a fallback, and a stopping condition."}

The first branch protects the smallest sufficient approach. The middle branches
map a diagnosed shortage to a broad method family without selecting a
particular technique. The final branch is deliberately different. When
checking or review already limits progress, increasing candidate throughput
worsens the system. The common endpoint makes the selection incomplete until
the approach has support, a total-cost case, a check matched to the
consequence, a fallback, and a stopping condition.

This guide can legitimately end with direct tool use, a conventional method,
or no added method. Combinations are justified only when the components remove
different limiting work and their interfaces and checks remain explicit.
The following tests develop the same sequence rather than introduce another
selection procedure.

**Required output and artifact.** Constructing an artifact, estimating a
consequence, selecting an experiment, and establishing a property are
different jobs. Text, graphs, spatial layouts, parameter vectors, and
experiment plans also have different structure. The method must fit both the
answer and the artifact rather than force every problem into a prompt.

**Legal space and known constraints.** Three enumerated cache sizes call for
direct comparison. A vast but regular mapping space may reward an analytical
model, heuristic, or optimizer, while sequential placement differs from a
static sweep because each action changes the choices that remain. Known
legality and feasibility rules should constrain the action space or run as
deterministic checks before the study spends scarce evaluations rediscovering
them. Unknown feasibility may instead justify prediction or selective tool
work, provided the later check remains explicit.

**Data, matching conditions, and evaluator.** Prediction requires observations
from matching workloads, design regions, tools, process conditions, and
representations. Those conditions define the predictor's support and determine
where its estimate may be used. Generation requires enough constraints to
define useful artifacts. Optimization requires an objective, legal actions,
and feedback. The evaluator must then observe the property the method claim
needs. A compiler can reject malformed code, a simulator can return behavior
for stated conditions, a solver can check encoded properties, and a
physical-design flow can expose implementation failures. A generated checker
is not automatically independent because it may repeat the generator's
assumptions or omissions.

**Total cost and deployment conditions.** Count setup, calibration, inference,
tool time, licenses, failed runs, checking, and expert review. Generation is
not cheap when every candidate is expensive to inspect, and prediction is not
efficient when calibration consumes the evaluations it was meant to save.
Latency and locality also matter. An offline predictor may train for hours and
answer quickly, while a compiler pass or interactive tool has a tighter
response limit. Proprietary RTL, foundry data, and licensed reports may require
local execution.

**Support, reversibility, and review capacity.** A method may work only for
particular workloads, design regions, process assumptions, or artifact forms.
State those limits before use. A disposable suggestion tolerates different
failure behavior from an automated RTL edit or a choice that reaches
fabrication. As reversal becomes slower or more expensive, the method needs
stronger constraints and checks. It is useful only when the work saved exceeds
the work handed to the next step; more candidates can make a review-limited
study slower.

The diagnosis should be repeated after the chosen approach changes the work.
A generator may remove a shortage of candidates and expose expensive
evaluation. A predictor may make screening cheap and expose overloaded review.
The method that was useful before that change may no longer be useful after it.

ArchGym gives an empirical reason not to canonize one search method. Under
equal sample budgets, reinforcement learning[^fn-ml-reinforcement-learning-c05],
Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and a random walker traded places
across architecture environments; no one method dominated every design space
[@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. The
result is not a universal ranking. It shows that the design space, environment,
tuning effort, and evaluation budget are part of method fit.

[^fn-ml-reinforcement-learning-c05]: **Reinforcement learning (RL)**: A
machine-learning technique that fits an action-selection policy from
interaction to increase accumulated reward [@SuttonBarto2018ReinforcementLearning].
In architecture design, it is an optimization technique for sequential
problems, and its reward remains a proxy for the declared engineering
objective.

Record the result of the selection sequence as an approach decision rather
than a method name. The fields in @tbl-method-role-limits make direct tools and
added methods comparable before work begins.

| **Field** | **Question to answer before selecting the approach** |
| --- | --- |
| **Job and question** | Which limiting work will this approach remove, and must it construct, estimate, select, or establish a property? |
| **Inputs and support** | Which represented state, artifacts, observations, workloads, design regions, and process assumptions may it use? |
| **Output** | What concrete result will it return? |
| **Search and allowed actions** | What structure does the legal space have, and which fields or artifacts may the method change or request? |
| **Evaluator and later checks** | Which evaluator can reject a bad output, what does it observe, and which stronger checks remain? |
| **Cost and latency** | What setup, calibration, inference, tool execution, checking, review, and response time will it consume? |
| **Confidentiality and locality** | Which inputs may leave the project boundary, and where must the technique execute? |
| **Reliability and reversibility** | What failure rate can the role tolerate, what happens when it fails, and how costly is reversal? |
| **Stop** | When is the job complete, unsupported, uneconomic, or out of budget? |

: **An approach decision is more than a method name.** These fields make a
direct tool path or an added method comparable before work begins, regardless
of whether its concrete technique is conventional, learned, or hybrid.
{#tbl-method-role-limits tbl-colwidths="[23,67]"}

These fields preserve the decisions already made about the job, support,
output, legal actions, evaluator, cost, deployment conditions, and failure
consequences. If two approaches cannot be stated in these same terms, their
method names do not yet make them comparable.

::: {.callout-engineer-move title="State every method claim concretely"}
For every method, state the artifact or parameter it changes, the interface it
uses, the feedback it receives, the check that can reject its output, and the
later decision that may use the result. A concrete sentence might read, "The
method may select only among the represented L2 capacities, `SIM-A` evaluates
the requested configurations, and the study compares their returned frame-time
distributions under the declared conditions."
:::

The declaration is incomplete until the study prices the feedback each
approach needs. Setup, tool calls, failed runs, licenses, and expert review can
dominate the apparent cost of the method itself.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

### Method Cost and Evaluation Capacity {#sec-sample-efficiency-under-expensive-feedback}

Every approach consumes more than compute. Its cost includes setup,
calibration, candidate construction, inference or search, tool execution,
licenses where relevant, failed runs, checking, and expert review. The useful
quantity is the expected cost of obtaining a result that can change the study
decision.

The study must therefore state how many tool evaluations and checks it can
afford, how long they may take, what they cost, which fidelity each uses, and
how much expert review capacity is available. Failed attempts consume the same
finite resources.

These constraints separate small studies from large searches. Three legal cache
capacities can be enumerated. Reported or computed accelerator and
tensor-program scale anchors can reach hundreds of millions to more than
$10^{18}$ possibilities
[@KwonEtAl2019MAESTRO; @ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM;
@ParasharEtAl2019Timeloop]. In the larger spaces, analytical pruning,
deterministic legality checks, heuristics, prediction, or optimization may save
expensive evaluations. In the smaller space, the same machinery can cost more
than it saves. @sec-evaluation-capacity-bounds-search computes a smaller
cross-product explicitly and separates candidate count from evaluation
capacity. These independent design-space anchors motivate search, but they do
not say how many evaluations a particular study can afford or how quickly its
pre-review tool path can settle them.

Candidate count alone does not reveal whether the declared tool path can absorb
the work before review. An illustrative pre-review tool-path capacity model
makes that question explicit. Let $g$ be the rate at which candidates enter
the tool path. For tool stage $i$, let $c_i$ be the number of parallel slots,
$t_i$ the mean time spent on one candidate, and $p_i$ the conditional fraction
that advances after that stage. The stage capacity is

$$
\mu_i = \frac{c_i}{t_i}.
$$

The offered load arriving at stage $i$ is

$$
\lambda_i =
g \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j,
$$

and its utilization is

$$
\rho_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\mu_i}.
$$

Under the model's feed-forward, steady-rate assumptions, each stage needs
$\rho_i < 1$. Above one, work arrives faster than the stage can settle it, so
its queue grows [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems]. Operating exactly at the bound
leaves no headroom for variable service time, retries, or shared-resource
delays. The corresponding first-order input-rate bound is

$$
g <
\min_i
\left(
\frac{\mu_i}
{\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} p_j}
\right).
$$

Consider an illustrative path receiving 32 candidates per day
(@tbl-candidate-check-capacity). A one-minute structural screen advances one
quarter of its inputs. Four parallel eight-hour simulations advance one tenth
of the candidates they receive. One 24-hour implementation screen advances
half of its inputs. The modeled path stops before architect review, whose
project-specific capacity must still be included in the approach decision.

```{python}
#| echo: false
candidate_rate = 32.0
structural_capacity = 24.0 * 60.0
simulation_capacity = 4.0 * (24.0 / 8.0)
implementation_capacity = 1.0
structural_advance = 0.25
simulation_advance = 0.10
implementation_advance = 0.50

structural_load = candidate_rate / structural_capacity
simulation_arrival = candidate_rate * structural_advance
simulation_load = simulation_arrival / simulation_capacity
implementation_arrival = simulation_arrival * simulation_advance
implementation_load = implementation_arrival / implementation_capacity
finalist_rate = (
    candidate_rate
    * structural_advance
    * simulation_advance
    * implementation_advance
)
```

| **Tool stage before review** | **Parallel slots $c_i$** | **Mean time $t_i$** | **Capacity $\mu_i$** | **Conditional advance $p_i$** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Structural and legality screen | 1 | 1 minute | 1,440/day | 0.25 |
| Cycle-level simulation | 4 | 8 hours | 12/day | 0.10 |
| Implementation screen | 1 | 24 hours | 1/day | 0.50 |

: **An illustrative pre-review tool-path capacity model exposes the active tool
limit.** The values are not measurements of a particular tool flow. They make
the load calculation inspectable. {#tbl-candidate-check-capacity
tbl-colwidths="[30,16,18,18,18]"}

The structural screen receives all 32 candidates per day and operates at
$32/1{,}440$, or `{python} f"{100 * structural_load:.1f}%"`, utilization.
`{python} f"{simulation_arrival:g}"` candidates per day reach simulation, which
operates at `{python} f"{100 * simulation_load:.1f}%"`. Only
`{python} f"{implementation_arrival:g}"` candidates per day reach the
implementation screen, which operates at
`{python} f"{100 * implementation_load:.0f}%"`. Implementation is therefore the
active capacity limit even though simulation handles more work. The expected
finalist rate after all three stages is

$$
q =
g \prod_i p_i.
$$

For the illustrative values, this is
`{python} f"{finalist_rate:.2f}"` finalists per day. That product is a flow
calculation, not the probability that a finalist is correct. It is also not
architecture-decision throughput. A supported decision may require several
finalists, a matched baseline, additional checks, and architect review.
Branching, return paths, correlated failures, variable service times, and
shared licenses require a richer model. Until project-specific review capacity
is included, this pre-review model cannot establish total evaluation capacity
or decision capacity.

The simple calculation is still useful for method choice. Generation tends to
increase $g$. An early deterministic screen can reduce the load passed
forward. Prediction consumes calibration and later confirmation work while
potentially reducing expensive evaluations. Optimization decides how to spend
the available evaluation capacity. When a modeled tool stage is saturated,
adding candidate production cannot remove the bottleneck. The same consequence
applies if separately assessed project review is saturated. The study must
reduce incoming work, reduce service time, add justified capacity, or change
what needs the scarce check.

Recorded evaluation costs can guide that choice. A simulator result, warning,
failed run, synthesis report,
measurement, or expert review can reduce uncertainty relevant to the decision.
One synthesis run that distinguishes the two leading candidates may be worth
more than another hundred proxy scores that preserve their ranking. The
architect should ask which uncertainty the next evaluation can resolve, whether
that result could change the candidate ranking or claim, and what the
evaluation will cost. Raw run count is not the objective.

Treating generation as free hides checking and review. Treating prediction as
free hides calibration. Treating optimization as free hides the evaluations it
spends.

Feedback cost creates several recurring choices without imposing a hierarchy.
A few legal configurations and cheap checks favor enumeration or direct tool
use. A cheap conventional screen is useful only if it preserves the candidates
that matter near the decision boundary. Observations from matching workloads,
design regions, tools, process conditions, and representations can justify
prediction only when calibration and confirmation cost less than direct
evaluation. A missing artifact can justify generation only when checking it is
economical. A legal space larger than the evaluation budget can justify
optimization only when the objective is meaningful and the search retains a
transparent baseline and explicit stop.

The value of each evaluation also depends on what the environment records.
Workload identity, candidate state, tool warnings, failure reasons, and
evaluation conditions make a result reusable.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces defines how the environment
captures those returns. At this stage, the approach decision needs only to budget
for them.

The next three sections develop the families without implying an execution
order.


## Prediction and World Models {#sec-prediction-estimating-behavior-before-full-evaluation}

Prediction is useful when candidates already exist but a decision-relevant
consequence is expensive to obtain. A predictor may estimate performance,
power, congestion, feasibility risk, candidate rank, or the effect of an
action before every candidate receives the stronger evaluation. Architects
used regression and predictive design-space models for this purpose long
before large language models became common
[@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @LeeBrooks2006RegressionModeling].

A predictor must estimate a consequence the decision actually uses. Its
technique should match the applicable workloads, design regions, tools, process
conditions, and representation (@tbl-prediction-techniques). An analytical
model or regression may fit sparse, structured data. Tree-based methods can fit
tabular parameters and interactions. A Gaussian process is a regression model
that fits a mean and uncertainty from observed points; it can guide
sample-conscious selection in a moderate-dimensional search. Neural and
sequence models require enough data from matching conditions to justify their
flexibility. A graph neural network can retain connectivity that flat features
discard, as in congestion prediction from a netlist
[@KirbyEtAl2019CongestionNet].

| **Predictive technique** | **Strong fit** | **Main reason to reject it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical or mechanistic cost model | Known relationships, limited data, and a need for inspectable assumptions. | The omitted interaction controls the decision. |
| Linear, polynomial, or regularized regression | Stable tabular features and a relationship that can be represented with modest complexity. | The response changes sharply or important structure is absent from the features. |
| Decision trees, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees | Tabular parameters, nonlinear interactions, and mixed feature types. | The method extrapolates into a design region unsupported by observations. |
| Gaussian process | Costly evaluations, moderate dimension, and a need to couple prediction with uncertainty-aware selection. | The space or dataset makes the surrogate costly or poorly matched. |
| Neural model | Large datasets from matching conditions and nonlinear behavior that simpler models do not capture. | Data coverage, latency, or confidentiality does not support training or use. |
| Sequence or transformer model | Programs, traces, reports, or time-dependent behavior whose order and long-range context matter. | The representation, dataset, or deployment budget cannot support the added flexibility. |
| Graph neural network | Netlists, dependency graphs, and other objects where connectivity carries the signal. | Node and edge features omit the property that controls the consequence. |
| Hybrid or simulator-corrected model | A useful analytical or low-fidelity model exists but has a repeatable residual error. | The correction data do not match the current tool, workload, or design region. |
| Transition or world model | Actions change later state and planning across several steps has value. | Independent candidate scoring or direct feedback is sufficient. |

: **Predictive techniques differ in the structure and support they require.**
This lecture-level selection heuristic follows the architecture consequence,
representation, data, and evaluation cost rather than asserting a general
model ranking.
{#tbl-prediction-techniques tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

Each row ties a represented relationship to a reason the technique might fit
and a condition that should rule it out. More flexible models do
not dominate simpler ones. A regression can be the stronger choice when data
are scarce and the relationship is stable, while a graph model is justified
only when connectivity carries information that the decision needs.

> **Transition model.** A transition model predicts how selected design state
> or a decision-relevant consequence may change after a permitted action or
> sequence of actions under stated conditions.

> **Architecture world model.** In this lecture, an architecture world model
> is a learned predictor of how represented design state, a permitted action,
> and stated conditions affect a later state or measured behavior. This is the
> lecture's architecture-specific working definition, informed by the broader
> learned-world-model lineage [@HaSchmidhuber2018WorldModels]. It is one kind
> of predictive technique, not a fourth method family or one universal model
> of architecture.

Consider sequential macro placement. The represented partial floorplan and a
legal macro-location action enter a transition predictor. A *bounded rollout*
is a predicted action sequence limited in how many alternatives it explores
and how many steps it predicts. A separate planner or optimizer uses the
transition predictor to compare those sequences and selects the first action.
Only that action reaches the authoritative placement tool. Its returned
observation replaces the predicted state as the current represented state and
triggers replanning from the real tool return. Deterministic checks still
exclude overlaps and blocked sites, while placement and routing remain
authoritative for congestion, timing, and routability.

This composition differs from two simpler choices. Independent static scoring
estimates each complete candidate without predicting how one action changes
later choices. A model-free policy maps the observed state directly to an
action without explicit predicted rollouts. A world model earns its added
predictor and planner only when the action horizon is long enough for sequence
effects to matter and bounded rollouts save enough real tool calls to offset
model fitting, accumulated prediction error, and checks of intermediate
states. Cheap tool feedback, a short horizon, rapidly growing rollout error,
or checking cost comparable to direct execution favors static scoring, a
model-free policy, or direct tool use. The world model remains a predictive
technique inside a composition, not a fourth family.

Different architecture jobs still need different state and consequence
models. A compiler-tuning model, a placement-transition model, and a
cache-performance model need not share one state or output. The authoritative
current state remains the represented project state from
@sec-data-representations-world-models, never an unconfirmed prediction.

A prediction remains separate from the later tool observation
(@fig-architecture-cost-model).

![**Prediction and observation follow different paths.** The represented state
and proposed action feed a scoped consequence model, including a transition
model when dynamics matter, that returns a prediction. The same state and action
feed a declared tool path that returns an observation. The study record keeps
both connected without treating the prediction as an
observation.](images/F5-architecture-world-model){#fig-architecture-cost-model
width="85%" fig-alt="A represented state and proposed action feed a scoped
consequence model and a separate tool path. The prediction and tool observation
remain distinct and both enter a versioned study record."}

In @fig-architecture-cost-model, the represented state and proposed action
feed two deliberately separate paths. The upper branch predicts a consequence within stated
limits. The lower branch asks the environment to invoke the real tool and
return an observation. Both results enter the study record, but in separate
fields. Agreement can support continued use within the model's stated support;
it does not validate the model generally. Disagreement can reveal model error, a
support failure, or a mismatch in the tool conditions that must be investigated
before the prediction guides another action.

## Predictor Support and Calibration {#support-limits}

The way a predictor will be used determines how it should be assessed. A
screening surrogate must preserve the ordering near the decision boundary, so
rank correlation and top-k recall[^fn-ml-top-k-recall-c05] can matter more than
global average error. Point accuracy still matters when a hard limit, such as
area or access time, decides feasibility. The assessment should match the
decision, candidate region, workload, and threshold rather than rely on one
aggregate score.

[^fn-ml-top-k-recall-c05]: **Top-k recall**: The fraction of the measured best
k candidates that also appear in the predictor's top k. It asks whether a
screen kept the designs worth evaluating, which differs from asking whether
all predicted values were numerically close.

Before a cheap predictor controls which candidates reach an expensive tool,
reserve a check batch from the candidate and condition region where the screen
will operate. Do not use that batch to fit or tune the predictor. Send it
through both paths. Decision-aligned ranking measures, including top-k recall,
help determine how many candidates must survive the screen to retain the
designs worth measuring. Weak recall requires a larger survivor set or
abandonment of the screen. The check runs count against the same evaluation
budget the predictor is intended to save.

Here, a calibration study compares a cheap predictor or proxy with a stronger
reference over the region where it will be used. The relevant comparison may
be numerical error near a threshold, ranking agreement for screening, or
interval coverage for an uncertainty claim.

This chapter uses calibration to decide whether a predictor is suitable for a
planned role and whether its reference runs fit within the study budget.
@sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration later asks the complementary
question: after the proxy has returned a value, which architecture conclusion
can that value support?

Prediction becomes dangerous when an optimizer sends it into a design or
workload region unlike its calibration data. Uncertainty estimates should not
be assumed to detect that support failure; they remain outputs of a model whose
assumptions may already have stopped matching the study.

A learned world model adds a sequence-specific version of this problem. An
acceptable error after one permitted action can accumulate across a longer
sequence or move the predicted state outside its calibrated region. The study
should qualify the sequence length and compare predicted intermediate states
with real tool observations before using them to choose later actions.

Conformal prediction[^fn-stats-conformal-prediction-c05], for example, can
attach a calibrated interval to a surrogate under an exchangeability
assumption[^fn-stats-exchangeability-c05] and a chosen nonconformity
score[^fn-stats-nonconformity-score-c05] [@LeiEtAl2018Conformal]. The guarantee
is marginal and depends on those assumptions. It does not promise coverage in
every design-space region, and it no longer applies after the relevant
exchangeability assumption fails.

[^fn-stats-conformal-prediction-c05]: **Conformal prediction**: A statistical technique that produces prediction sets or intervals from a model, with finite-sample coverage guarantees under an exchangeability assumption. Here, a calibrated interval may be used to prune, defer, or escalate a candidate, but it does not authorize a design decision.

[^fn-stats-exchangeability-c05]: **Exchangeability**: A statistical property where the joint distribution of a sequence of random variables is invariant to their permutation, a weaker assumption than being independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.). Architecture workloads, tools, and process corners may violate it, so a conformal interval must be audited rather than trusted.

[^fn-stats-nonconformity-score-c05]: **Nonconformity score**: A function that
measures how poorly a fitted model agrees with an observed calibration case. In
split-conformal regression, it is often the absolute residual between the
prediction and observation. In the fixed-width construction shown here, a
chosen quantile of those calibration scores fixes the interval width.

Coverage that is acceptable within a calibration region can collapse after the
response changes even though the interval itself does not change
(@fig-ch05-conformal-coverage). An occasional miss is compatible with 90
percent marginal coverage and does not establish drift. The relationship to
inspect is the sustained mismatch after the support assumption fails.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch05-conformal-coverage
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A calibrated interval depends on its support assumptions:** Constructed illustration of a split-conformal band around a latency-like surrogate. Inside the calibration regime, empirical coverage is close to the nominal 90% level. After the response changes, the exchangeability assumption no longer holds and most observations leave the unchanged band. A sustained mismatch should stop predictor-based screening and prompt review. All values are synthetic and illustrative.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of synthetic latency-like data with a fixed-width conformal prediction band around a surrogate curve. In the calibrated support region on the left, nearly all points fall inside the band; in the distribution-shift region on the right, observed behavior rises away from the unchanged band and most points escape it, showing coverage collapse."

import math
import random

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Constructed illustration: every value is synthetic, generated in this cell
# with a fixed seed; no real system was measured. The split-conformal recipe
# (calibration residual quantile -> fixed-width band) follows the conformal
# prediction pattern cited in the text.
rng = random.Random(20260713)
SHIFT_X = 6.0
NOISE = 0.32
X_MAX = 10.0

def surrogate(x):
    # The pattern the surrogate learned inside the calibrated region.
    return 4.0 + 1.8 * math.sin(0.9 * x) + 0.25 * x

def truth(x):
    # Beyond the calibrated region the workload regime changes.
    drift = 1.1 * (x - SHIFT_X) ** 1.25 if x > SHIFT_X else 0.0
    return surrogate(x) + drift

def observe(x):
    return truth(x) + rng.gauss(0.0, NOISE)

# Split conformal: the 90% quantile of absolute calibration residuals from the
# supported region sets a fixed band half-width q.
cal_x = [rng.uniform(0.0, SHIFT_X) for _ in range(60)]
cal_scores = sorted(abs(observe(x) - surrogate(x)) for x in cal_x)
q = cal_scores[math.ceil(0.9 * (len(cal_scores) + 1)) - 1]

test_in = [(x, observe(x)) for x in [0.15 + i * (SHIFT_X - 0.3) / 24 for i in range(25)]]
test_out = [(x, observe(x)) for x in [SHIFT_X + 0.15 + i * (X_MAX - SHIFT_X - 0.3) / 24 for i in range(25)]]
cov_in = sum(abs(y - surrogate(x)) <= q for x, y in test_in) / len(test_in)
cov_out = sum(abs(y - surrogate(x)) <= q for x, y in test_out) / len(test_out)

xs = [i * X_MAX / 400 for i in range(401)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.9, 2.55))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.11, right=0.97, top=0.86, bottom=0.19)

ax.fill_between(xs, [surrogate(x) - q for x in xs], [surrogate(x) + q for x in xs],
                color=COLORS["blue"], alpha=0.16, linewidth=0, zorder=1)
ax.plot(xs, [surrogate(x) for x in xs], color=COLORS["blue"], linewidth=1.1, zorder=2)
ax.plot(xs, [truth(x) for x in xs], color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.9,
        linestyle=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=2)

ax.scatter([x for x, _ in test_in], [y for _, y in test_in], s=9,
           color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
miss = [(x, y) for x, y in test_out if abs(y - surrogate(x)) > q]
hit = [(x, y) for x, y in test_out if abs(y - surrogate(x)) <= q]
ax.scatter([x for x, _ in hit], [y for _, y in hit], s=9, color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=3)
ax.scatter([x for x, _ in miss], [y for _, y in miss], s=11, color=COLORS["red"], zorder=3)

ax.axvline(SHIFT_X, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.7, linestyle="--", zorder=1)
ymin, ymax = ax.get_ylim()
ax.set_ylim(ymin, ymax + 1.2)
ax.text(SHIFT_X / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 0.35, "calibrated support", ha="center",
        va="top", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["workload_ink"])
ax.text((SHIFT_X + X_MAX) / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 0.35, "changed workload regime",
        ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["constraints_ink"])
ax.text(SHIFT_X / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 1.15,
        f"empirical coverage ≈ {cov_in:.0%}\n(nominal 90%)", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["workload_ink"])
ax.text((SHIFT_X + X_MAX) / 2, ax.get_ylim()[1] - 1.15,
        f"same band width,\ncoverage ≈ {cov_out:.0%}", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["constraints_ink"])

ax.annotate("surrogate ± conformal band", (1.7, surrogate(1.7) + q),
            textcoords="offset points", xytext=(-2, 5), fontsize=5.6,
            color=COLORS["workload_ink"])
ax.annotate("observed behavior", (8.2, truth(8.2)), textcoords="offset points",
            xytext=(-58, 2), fontsize=5.6, color=COLORS["muted"])

ax.set_xlabel("workload / design parameter (synthetic units)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("latency-like metric\n(synthetic units)", fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlim(0, X_MAX)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.5, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The vertical boundary separates calibrated support from a changed workload
regime. On the left, the blue observations
mostly remain inside the fixed band around the surrogate. On the right, the
observed response separates from that band and the red misses accumulate,
while the band itself remains unchanged. This synthetic construction does not
estimate the failure rate of a real architecture predictor. It demonstrates
why nominal marginal coverage inside one support region cannot justify
screening after the relevant workload or design response changes.

The response to a support failure must be planned rather than automatic.
Possible actions include stopping predictor-based screening, requesting a
limited number of stronger evaluations, recalibrating with compatible data, or
dropping the predictor. Each action spends budget and may change the study
plan. Before use, the study should state the audit window and the recall,
coverage, or threshold-error condition that stops predictor-based work. The
synthetic illustration does not supply a universal threshold.
@sec-feedback-verification-trust develops how the returned comparisons
establish whether a predictor remains useful.

`XR-L2-CAP-A` declares no live observations from matching workloads, design
regions, tools, process conditions, and representations. Its three direct
candidates and four cycle-level executions make predictor setup harder to
justify than direct comparison. If a later study expands the cache space and
declares matching results, prediction may become useful. That future condition
does not make it useful now.

A predictor should stop when compatible calibration cannot be established,
when the candidate leaves its stated support, when its error is too large for
the decision, or when direct evaluation becomes cheaper than maintaining the
model. The planned later check must remain visible because the predictor
estimates a result rather than replacing the tool or measurement that the
study requested.

## Generation Constructs Missing Artifacts

Generation helps when a needed candidate or artifact does not exist. A
generator can propose a simulator configuration, RTL fragment, testbench,
compiler schedule, kernel, placement, or experiment. It is not the default
method for every design task. When candidates already exist, prediction,
optimization, a conventional method, or direct evaluation may address the
actual missing capability with less work.

The artifact determines which generative technique is plausible. Templates,
grammars, rules, program synthesis, compiler passes, and parameterized
generators fit precisely structured artifacts. An autoregressive code model
constructs a sequence one token at a time from the preceding tokens, which fits
specifications, RTL, tests, and scripts. Constrained decoding blocks a next
token when it would violate an encoded grammar or schema, reducing syntactically
invalid work before compilation. Retrieval can supply current project documents
or examples to those techniques, but it remains a supporting capability rather
than a generation family. Graph generators fit connectivity. A
diffusion-based spatial generator begins with a noisy spatial proposal and
iteratively refines it, which can fit placement and floorplan construction.

The artifact structure narrows the choice
(@tbl-generation-techniques).

| **Artifact or problem** | **Likely construction path** | **What the path can enforce or use** | **External check still required** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Precisely structured configuration or program | Template, grammar-guided generator, solver, compiler pass, or program synthesis | Encoded syntax, types, and stated constraints | Intended semantics and implementation behavior |
| RTL, test, script, or compiler code | Autoregressive code model or LLM, optionally with constrained decoding | Supplied context and encoded token or schema restrictions | Elaboration, function, synthesis, timing, and other artifact-specific properties |
| Project-specific text or code | Retrieval-supported generation | Current retrieved documents and examples, subject to their provenance and coverage | Source consistency and the checks required by the generated artifact |
| Netlist or connectivity object | Graph-generative or graph-conditioned method | Represented nodes, edges, and graph constraints | Electrical, functional, timing, and physical properties |
| Placement or floorplan | Diffusion or another spatial generator | Spatial proposal distribution, fixed block geometry, and encoded placement constraints | Legalization, routing, timing, power, and manufacturability |
| Mixed hard and learned constraints | Learned proposal followed by a solver, compiler, deterministic builder, or repair step | Hard constraints encoded by the conventional component and patterns learned from data from matching conditions | Every relevant property not established by the encoded constraints |

: **Generative techniques should match the artifact and its available
constraints.** Structure that can be enforced during construction reduces bad
work but does not remove the property-specific checks that establish whether
the artifact is usable. {#tbl-generation-techniques
tbl-colwidths="[21,24,27,28]"}

Constraint handling determines how much bad work reaches later tools.
Constrained decoding can guarantee membership in an encoded grammar
[@WillardLouf2023GuidedGeneration; @GengEtAl2023GrammarConstrained], but it
cannot establish elaboration, functional correctness, routability, timing, or
power. A spatial generator has the same boundary. It can propose a layout, and
later tools determine which declared physical conditions that layout satisfies
[@LeeEtAl2025DiffusionPlacement]. Hybrid construction can combine a learned
proposal with a solver, compiler, deterministic builder, or repair step, but
the final artifact still needs the property-specific check.

The generator therefore needs a scoped input, legal actions, and inexpensive
early checks. A syntactically valid RTL fragment may still fail simulation,
synthesis, routing, or timing closure. A generated dataflow may be legal while
creating unacceptable movement or buffering. Generation is useful only when
the project can reject poor proposals before they consume the scarce tool and
review budget. When the generated artifact is executable or synthesizable,
functional correctness must be established before its performance is compared.

A generated checker is not automatically independent verification. A
generator that emits both RTL and its testbench may repeat the same
misinterpreted requirement in both artifacts. The checker can still expose
errors, but independence requires a sufficiently different oracle, tool,
implementation, or reviewer and an explicit account of the assumptions that
remain shared.

Generation should stop when the study has enough useful alternatives, when
checking or review becomes the new bottleneck, or when the generator repeatedly
leaves the represented action space. It must not widen that space silently.
For `XR-L2-CAP-A`, the proposal job is already complete because the legal
alternatives and their artifacts exist. Deterministic serialization and
configuration checks prepare those artifacts for the tools. A generator adds
no needed output. Proposing a new cache policy, associativity, NoC, or compiler
change would reopen the study rather than improve it.

Kernel generation makes the separation visible because a compute subsystem
depends on target-specific kernels that are both correct and efficient.
KernelBench, an evaluation framework for AI-generated code, asks language
models to produce GPU kernels for PyTorch workloads
[@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench]. Its harness compiles each candidate, checks
numerical correctness, and compares performance with the PyTorch Eager
baseline.

One attempt per task shows how sharply the candidate count falls from
attempted, to correct, to correct and faster
(@fig-ch05-kernel-funnel), for four models across three difficulty levels. The
dashed line marks attempted tasks,
the blue bars mark correct kernels, and the green bars mark kernels that are
both correct and faster than the baseline. The important relationship is the
drop between those three conditions. Generating code, producing correct code,
and improving performance are separate achievements.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch05-kernel-funnel
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Attempted is not correct, and correct is not fast:** One-shot KernelBench results for four language models across the benchmark's three difficulty levels, measured on an NVIDIA L40S GPU [@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench]. The dashed 100 percent line marks tasks attempted, not measured fluency or plausibility. The harness's correctness oracle passes far fewer candidates, and only a small fraction are both correct and faster than the PyTorch Eager baseline.
#|
#|   The paper prints no per-model compile rates, and these panels chart none of them; in the paper's separate 100-kernel error-analysis sample, 83 of 100 generated kernels compile and 73 execute before the correctness oracle prunes the set to 50. For Llama-3.1-70B at Level 1, the paper's Tables 8 and 9 report 26 percent and 27 percent, respectively; this figure uses Table 8's 26 percent value. Values transcribed from the paper's published single-attempt tables.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Three-panel grouped bar chart of one-shot KernelBench outcomes for Llama-3.1-70B, DeepSeek V3, OpenAI o1, and DeepSeek R1 at difficulty levels one, two, and three. In each panel a dashed line at one hundred percent marks tasks attempted; blue bars show the share passing the correctness oracle, from zero to sixty-seven percent, and green bars show the share both correct and faster than the PyTorch Eager baseline, from zero to thirty-six percent. Both bars sit far below the dashed line everywhere, and the fast share is always well below the correct share."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Source receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter6-kernelbench-funnel.csv
# KernelBench [@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench], single greedy attempt on NVIDIA
# L40S: one-shot correctness (fast_0, Tables 8 and 9) and correct-and-faster-
# than-PyTorch-Eager (fast_1, Table 1), percent of tasks per level.
# Per-model compile/execution rates are not printed in the paper (its Figure 3
# is unlabeled), so no compile-stage bars; the source record includes the paper's
# 100-kernel supplementary sample (83 compile / 73 execute / 50 correct) as
# context only.
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

with open(
    _root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter6-kernelbench-funnel.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    receipt_rows = list(csv.DictReader(fh))

model_order = [
    "Llama-3.1-70B Instruct",
    "DeepSeek V3",
    "OpenAI o1",
    "DeepSeek R1",
]
models = ["Llama\n3.1-70B", "DeepSeek\nV3", "OpenAI\no1", "DeepSeek\nR1"]

def receipt_values(metric, level):
    selected = {
        row["model"]: float(row["value_pct"])
        for row in receipt_rows
        if row["metric"] == metric and row["kernelbench_level"] == str(level)
    }
    if set(selected) != set(model_order):
        raise ValueError(f"Incomplete KernelBench receipt for {metric}, level {level}")
    return [selected[model] for model in model_order]

correct = {
    level: receipt_values("correct_one_shot", level)
    for level in (1, 2, 3)
}
fast1 = {
    level: receipt_values("correct_and_faster_than_eager", level)
    for level in (1, 2, 3)
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(5.15, 1.95), sharey=True)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.09, right=0.985, top=0.80, bottom=0.24, wspace=0.10)

width = 0.36
xs = range(len(models))
for ax, level in zip(axes, (1, 2, 3)):
    ax.axhline(100, color=COLORS["muted"], linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (4, 3)),
               zorder=1)
    ax.bar([x - width / 2 for x in xs], correct[level], width=width * 0.94,
           color=COLORS["blue"], zorder=2,
           label="correct" if level == 1 else None)
    ax.bar([x + width / 2 for x in xs], fast1[level], width=width * 0.94,
           color=COLORS["evidence"], zorder=2,
           label="correct and faster\nthan baseline" if level == 1 else None)
    ax.set_title(f"Level {level}", fontsize=6.6, pad=3)
    ax.set_xticks(list(xs))
    ax.set_xticklabels(models, fontsize=5.1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 112)
    ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55)
    for spine in ["top", "right"]:
        ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
axes[0].set_ylabel("share of tasks (%)", fontsize=6.4)
axes[0].annotate("task attempted", (0.05, 100), textcoords="offset points",
                 xytext=(0, 3), fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"])
fig.legend(loc="upper center", ncol=2, fontsize=6, frameon=False,
           bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0), handlelength=1.0, columnspacing=1.4)
plt.show()
```
Across every panel in @fig-ch05-kernel-funnel, the correct share sits well below
the attempted share, and the correct-and-faster share is smaller again. The
model ordering also changes with task difficulty. An architect cannot infer
kernel quality from fluency or from an overall model ranking. The generator
proposes code, while the harness determines correctness and the baseline
comparison determines whether the code is faster under the tested conditions.

A reusable KernelBench-style evaluation records the target platform,
correctness oracle, numerical tolerance, baseline, failed kernels, portability
limits, and the rejection rule for fast but incorrect code. When proposals already arrive faster
than they can be rejected, generating more only lengthens the backlog unless
checking capacity also improves.

A fair method comparison asks how the missing artifact is constructed, not
only whether the final artifact beats an execution baseline. PyTorch Eager
provides a useful performance reference for a generated kernel, but it does not
by itself represent the strongest practical conventional construction path. A
compiler, optimized library, parameterized template, or autotuning system may
already produce the needed kernel without learned generation.

The learned and conventional paths should therefore receive the same task
specification, target, semantics, numerical tolerance, permitted
transformations, online context, allowed tool feedback, and budget. Each arm's
pretrained model, compiler rules, optimized libraries, templates, and other
prebuilt assets must be declared rather than treated as identical starting
information. Both paths must pass the same compilation and correctness checks
before performance counts. Their costs include failed attempts, target
executions, setup, and expert review. The comparison can then ask whether
learned generation produces a correct and faster kernel, reaches a comparable
result with less total work, or supplies an artifact that the conventional
path cannot produce within the budget. KernelBench demonstrates the output
checks and candidate funnel, but it does not by itself settle this complete
construction comparison.

A prospective comparison plan shows the method-choice information that must be
fixed before execution (@tbl-generation-construction-pair). It asks both paths
to construct one fused layer-normalization forward kernel for the same pinned
shapes, data types, and target GPU. The available evidence does not identify a
strongest conventional constructor, model version, or defensible common
budget, so the result remains unresolved.

| **Aspect** | **Prospective matched-construction comparison** |
| --- | --- |
| **Artifact and semantics** | Pin one executable layer-normalization operation, tensor shapes, data types, numerical tolerance, and target GPU before selecting either constructor. |
| **Construction arms** | Predeclare one strongest practical library, compiler-fusion, parameterized-template, conventional-autotuning constructor, or fixed portfolio, and one code-generating model and version. Both receive the same operation and permitted tool returns. |
| **Shared tools and checks** | Both paths use the same compiler, correctness harness, tolerance, timing procedure, warm-up policy, and target executions. Incorrect or noncompiling artifacts cannot enter the performance comparison. |
| **Matched resources** | Pin the online context, wall-clock limit, target-execution allowance, and expert setup and repair allowance. Declare arm-specific pretrained models, libraries, compiler rules, templates, and other prebuilt assets. |
| **Recorded result** | Retain attempted artifacts, failures, target runs, accepted performance, tool and model cost, elapsed time, and expert work. Compare total work only after an artifact passes the shared checks, and leave the result unresolved if neither path succeeds within budget. |

: **A generation comparison must match construction paths, not only final
artifacts.** This prospective comparison identifies what must be pinned before a
learned and conventional construction pair can be compared.
{#tbl-generation-construction-pair tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

The shared compiler and correctness harness first determine whether either path
produced a usable kernel. Performance separates accepted artifacts only after
that check. A learned kernel that runs faster but consumes substantially more
construction and review effort is a tradeoff, not an automatic win.

The same test transfers to RTL. A learned RTL generator should be compared with
a serious parameterized generator, template, high-level synthesis path, or
solver-backed construction method under the same interface contract, allowed
changes, testbench, implementation tools, and engineering budget. The result
may favor the conventional path. Generation earns a role only when it supplies
needed work more effectively without weakening the checks that make the
artifact usable.

Chip-Chat, an interactive hardware design study, brings the same role
separation into RTL design [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat]. A language model
drafted Verilog for a small 8-bit processor that reached tapeout after a human
guided many revisions. Open-source simulation and synthesis tools returned
errors that could reject or redirect drafts, while the human designer decided
when a candidate was ready to advance. The example shows why generation cost
cannot be separated from checking cost. Whether that total cost is acceptable
depends on the artifact, tool latency, and available review capacity.

## Optimization Allocates Scarce Evaluations

Optimization is especially useful when the legal space is too large to
enumerate and the evaluation budget forces the study to choose which candidate
to try next. Reduced-space enumeration is a conventional comparison.
Deterministic heuristics, random search, Bayesian optimization, evolutionary
search, reinforcement learning, and constraint-based procedures provide other
options. The structure of the space and the feedback cost determine the fit.

Known legality and tool-discovered feasibility need different treatment. Known
constraints, such as an enumerated cache capacity or nonoverlap rule, should be
encoded in candidate construction or action operators when feasible, or applied
as a deterministic rejection or projection before scarce evaluation.
Placement, routing, timing, simulation, or implementation may expose additional
limits only after a tool runs. A valid completed result can label a candidate
feasible or infeasible only under the named tool, settings, effort, resource
budget, and stopping condition. A run stopped at a declared time or resource
limit returns incomplete or timeout feedback. For a timeout, completion time
may be right-censored at the limit only when the analysis defines a censoring
model; the timeout establishes only that completion exceeded the limit, not
its exact value. Other objectives remain incomplete or unobserved. A crash, stale
workspace, or missing artifact is instead an invalid or infrastructure result.
These outcomes should stay outside the ordinary objective channel unless the
optimization formulation models them explicitly. Repeated feasibility feedback
may justify constrained optimization or a separate feasibility predictor, but
the relevant design tool still establishes the scoped condition.

Selecting the best of many surrogate-scored candidates is itself biased. Even
when prediction errors average to zero, selection favors candidates whose
errors happened to be optimistic. The winner's predicted gain can therefore
exceed the later observed gain, with the gap tending to grow as the candidate
pool or score noise grows. This is the *optimizer's curse*
[@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. The plan should preserve the predicted
score, reserve independent confirmation appropriate to the variability and
decision, and report any shrinkage rather than presenting the selected
prediction as the final result.

### Balancing Exploration and Exploitation

Within a fixed search space, exploration and exploitation describe where an
optimizer spends its next evaluation. Exploitation samples where results
already look promising. Exploration samples less-understood parts of the same
declared space. Neither widens that space. A new topology, dataflow, ISA
extension, or cache policy would reopen study formulation and representation.

An acquisition rule combines the surrogate's predicted objective and
uncertainty to choose the next expensive evaluation
(@fig-bayesian-optimization).

```{python}
#| label: fig-bayesian-optimization
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Bayesian optimization allocates the next evaluation.** The surrogate mean predicts the objective, the shaded band shows uncertainty from sparse observations (widening away from observed points), and the acquisition function combines both to choose where to sample next, trading exploitation of high-mean regions against exploration of high-uncertainty ones. Illustrative one-parameter example.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked panels over a shared design-space axis. Top: a surrogate mean curve, a shaded uncertainty band, and three observation points. Bottom: an acquisition curve labeled at an exploit region, with an arrow marking the next evaluation as the combination of mean and uncertainty."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

# Illustrative 1-D Gaussian-process posterior with a radial-basis-function
# kernel and a small observation-noise term. Deterministic, with no random
# sampling. The acquisition is an upper-confidence bound (mean + 1.6 sigma).
apply_style()

def rbf_kernel(a, b, length_scale=1.35):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((a[:, None] - b[None, :]) / length_scale) ** 2)

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 400)
x_obs = np.array([1.2, 3.8, 7.2])
y_obs = np.array([0.28, 1.03, -0.48])

noise_variance = 0.0025
k_obs = rbf_kernel(x_obs, x_obs) + noise_variance * np.eye(len(x_obs))
k_cross = rbf_kernel(x_obs, x)
alpha = np.linalg.solve(k_obs, y_obs)
mean = k_cross.T @ alpha
posterior_covariance = rbf_kernel(x, x) - k_cross.T @ np.linalg.solve(k_obs, k_cross)
sigma = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.diag(posterior_covariance), 0.0, None))
kappa = 1.6
acq = mean + kappa * sigma

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(5.2, 3.5), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2.1, 1]}
)

ax1.fill_between(x, mean - sigma, mean + sigma, color=COLORS["workload"],
                 alpha=0.15, linewidth=0, label="Uncertainty")
ax1.plot(x, mean, color=COLORS["workload"], linewidth=1.8, label="Surrogate mean")
ax1.scatter(x_obs, y_obs, s=34, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["evidence"],
            edgecolor=COLORS["evidence_ink"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=4,
            label="Observations")
ax1.set_ylabel("Objective", fontsize=6.8)
ax1.tick_params(labelsize=6.0)
ax1.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handlelength=1.4,
           borderaxespad=0.2, labelspacing=0.35)
ax1.margins(y=0.18)

ax2.fill_between(x, acq.min() - 0.05, acq, color=COLORS["methods"],
                 alpha=0.18, linewidth=0)
ax2.plot(x, acq, color=COLORS["methods"], linewidth=1.7)
x_next = float(x[int(np.argmax(acq))])
ax2.scatter([x_next], [acq.max()], s=30, marker="s", facecolor=COLORS["methods"],
            edgecolor=COLORS["methods_ink"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=4)
ax2.text(3.8, acq.max() * 0.60, "Exploit\n(high mean)", ha="center",
         fontsize=5.6, color=COLORS["methods_ink"], fontweight="bold")
ax2.annotate("Next evaluation\n(mean + uncertainty)", xy=(x_next, acq.max()),
             xytext=(8.4, acq.max() * 0.52), ha="center", fontsize=5.6,
             color=COLORS["methods_ink"], fontweight="bold",
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["methods_ink"], lw=0.8))
ax2.set_ylabel("Acquisition", fontsize=6.8)
ax2.set_xlabel("Design space (one parameter)", fontsize=6.8)
ax2.tick_params(labelsize=6.0)
ax2.set_yticks([])

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11, hspace=0.12)
```

The upper panel separates three observations from the surrogate mean and its
shaded uncertainty band. The band narrows at measured points and widens where
the design space is less observed. The lower panel combines that mean and
uncertainty in an acquisition curve whose marked peak selects the next
evaluation [@SrinivasEtAl2010GPUCB]. The upper and lower panels therefore
separate consequence prediction from evaluation selection.

The band in the figure represents the model's uncertainty from sparse
observations. It does not represent every source of run-to-run variability.
The surrogate and acquisition rule perform different jobs and should be
inspectable separately even when one implementation packages them together.
The optimizer does not define the architecture question or authorize the
result. It selects candidates or evaluations within a declared action space,
objective, constraints, stopping condition, and limits on the number, latency,
cost, and fidelity of evaluations and reviews.

Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization[^fn-ml-multi-fidelity-bo-c05] extends the
choice to include evaluation fidelity [@KandasamyEtAl2017MultiFidelityBO]. The
execution request should ask the environment to retain the acquisition rule,
fidelity choice, assumptions, returned result, rejected alternatives, and
escalation threshold.

[^fn-ml-multi-fidelity-bo-c05]: **Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization**:
Jointly chooses which design to evaluate and at which fidelity level, trading
expected information against cost. The selection policy does not decide what
claim either feedback level can establish.

### Selecting a Search Procedure

The structure of the represented space helps select the search procedure, not
the procedure's popularity. Enumeration and deterministic heuristics are strong
choices for small or well-structured spaces. Bayesian optimization can fit
expensive black-box evaluation in low or moderate dimension when useful
observations and a suitable surrogate are available
[@JonesSchonlauWelch1998EGO;
@SnoekLarochelleAdams2012BayesianOptimization]. Evolutionary search can fit
mixed discrete spaces with legal variation operators and enough parallel
budget. Constraint-based search fits properties that can be stated
exhaustively.

When a legal space has many declared parameters, a screening experiment can be
useful before the main search. The study deliberately varies a limited set of
factor combinations to estimate which main parameters change the
decision-relevant result enough to justify more evaluation
[@PlackettBurman1946Design]. This is an option, not a required stage. Strong
interactions, discrete topology changes, or a screen built on a weak proxy can
make the apparent ranking misleading. A parameter that looks unimportant
inside the screened region is not proven irrelevant elsewhere.

When objectives and constraints admit a useful algebraic formulation,
mathematical programming or constraint solving can exploit that structure
directly. This is often preferable to paying for a learned search procedure.
The solver establishes only what the formulation contains, so omitted physical
or software effects still require the relevant later checks.

Reinforcement learning has a distinct fit. It is most defensible when the
problem is genuinely sequential, an action changes the state, later choices
depend on earlier ones, and repeated interaction is affordable. Macro placement
is one such formulation. A placement policy chooses one location at a time, and
the partial floorplan becomes the next state.

Sequential placement differs from a static parameter search because each macro
location changes the state for the next choice. The AlphaChip formulation
connects those repeated actions to terminal proxy feedback
(@fig-alphachip-placement) [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement].

![**Reinforcement learning places macros one at a time.** A placement policy
chooses each macro's location on the outbound action lane. The updated partial
floorplan returns on a separate next-state lane. After the final macro, an
approximate standard-cell placement supports a weighted proxy cost based on
density, congestion, and wirelength. The terminal reward is the negative of
that cost.
](images/F5c-macro-placement){#fig-alphachip-placement width="85%"
fig-alt="A loop with separate lanes for the placement policy's outbound macro-location action and the partial floorplan's inbound next state. After all macros are placed, approximate standard-cell placement precedes the density, congestion, and wirelength proxy cost, whose negative becomes the terminal reward."}
